A mob overpowered the sheriff at Camden, Ark., and took out and hanged two negroes who had murdered a white man.

R. Jennyss, her husband and Will Wilkinson were held for trial at Asheville, N. C., for the killing of Mrs. Jennyss.

George Maechel, killed Theo. Korkham, at Bean lake a Kansas City, Mo., resort. Maechel afterwards committed suicide.

George Thomas shot and fatally wounded Annie Lowe, at a negro dance near Philadelphia because she would not dance with him.

Two brothers named Robinall got into a quarrel at a dance near Findlay Ohio, and one used brass knuckles with fatal effect.

Clarence Barr, the Chinatown guide, died at San Francisco. C. J. Henderson, the Rochester traveling salesman, is charged with the murder.

Frank Botvick was murdered by an unknown stranger in Leadville. Col. The sheriff is looking for the man.

George Jessup and Joseph Boyer of Lafayette, Ind., had a dispute in Brookston. Boyer stabbed Jessup in the face. Jessup shot Boyer three times. Boyer will die.

Dr. Eddmon, on trial at Bowling Green, Ohio, for being the principal criminal in the Peany murder case, was found not guilty. Mrs. Eddmon was also discharged.

Jacob Rothschild, a salesman for a music company, was shot twice, and instantly killed by Dr. John White, a well-known physician at Memphis, Tenn. Nothing is known of the nature of their quarrel.

cato-graves-waterford-1895-08-24.A1:
DEFEATED LYNCHERS.
The Manner in Which the Prisoners Were Carried to Columbia.
Columbia, S. C., Aug. 24.—The six negroes brought to Columbia from Carleton county to prevent their being lynched have been safely lodged in the state penitentiary. The story told by Deputy Sheriff Black, who was in command of the squad of deputies in charge of the negroes, is a wierd one. He says the party left Walterboro with the prisoners at about 5 o'clock in the afternoon, after the sheriff had received information that a mob from Hampton county were on their way to lynch the negroes. Four men from Hampton county saw the deputies leave town, and were supposed to have given information to their confederates, who were waiting for night to come on before they began their attack upon the jail. It then became a race between the deputies and the would-be lynchers. By a most circuitous route through the swamps, crossing a river several times, all pursuit was foiled, and the deputies with their prisoners arrived at the Ashepoo trestle, where they flagged the fast mail for Charleston, wither they went with their charges. The negroes were brought to Columbia via Sumter so as to avoid possible interception on the line of the Soth Carolina and Georgia railway.
cato-graves-waterford-1895-08-24.A2:
SOUTH CAROLINA.
SOUTH CAROLINA.

Columbia is soon to have a new city directory.

Adjutant and Inspector General General Watts is out on a tour of inspection.

The hotels are making ready for the delegates to the constitutional convention.

The numerous colleges of Columbia are beginning to get ready for the influx of students.

The case against T. J. Kirven, for stealing the registration books of the Darlington precinct was heard Saturday before Trial Justice Warr. The case was dismissed.

Wm. P. Huff has discovered gold in paying quantities on his farm near Piedmont. Panning has been attended with such successful results that parties interested think of putting in improved machinery at once.

The Rev. J. L. Tillman, an evangelist, is conducting a series of gospel meetings in the court house in Sumter. His meetings are attended by comparatively good audiences, and considerable interest is being manifested.
The Baptist Association at Spartanburg drew a large crowd the first day, and the church was filled Thursday, although it was raining. Maj. A. B. Woodruff was elected moderator. For several years a layman has presided over the meetings of the association. They adjourned yesterday.

Dave Snoddy, a 64-year-old colored man, was killed by a train on the Southern Friday, near Fair Forest, in Spartanburg county. The old man was seen by the engineer just as he rounded a curve. He seemed dazed, and made no effort to get out of the way. It was impossible for the engineer to stop his train in time to save him.

Gov. Evans has appointed Gen. C. I. Walker and Messrs. C. K. Hudson and J. D. McLucas to locate the position of the South Carolina troops which took part in the battles of Chickamauga and Chattanooga. These gentlemen will also take steps looking to the erection of suitable monuments to mark the locations of the troops.

Anderson Corr. Columbia State: In a mass meeting of the citizens Saturday, it was decided to build a $250,000 cotton mill. R. S. Hill and I. J. Fretwell will be at the head of the enterprise, and this fact assures its success. Liberal subscriptions have already been made and there is no doubt that the full amount of the capital stock will be secured immediately.

The building of a railroad from Spartanburg to Henrietta Cotton Mill is now talked about. The S. A. L. is building a mile branch from this road to Henrietta. It is said that the contract is out for building the gap between Marion, N. C., and the Tennessee line across the mountains. When that is finished it is claimed by the advocates of the road that it will give Spartanburg another outlet to the west. It is only about 24 miles to Henrietta.

Gov. Evans has received a pathetic letter from a negro in Barnwell imploring him "for God's sake" to protect them against the "white caps," and goes on to relate how a negro was tied up and beaten several weeks ago. This is the same case that has already been called to the governor's attention, and he instructed Sheriff Lancaster to investigate it. The sheriff has written that he is ferreting out the facts, but that in the meantime all is quiet.—Register.

Columbia Corr. Sunday News: One of the most interesting matters that will come up before the constitutional convention will be how to provide for the support of public schools for a long time there has been a sentiment against the retention of the two-mill school tax in the constitution, and efforts have already been made to have it eliminated from the present constitution. Some want the two-mill tax taken out of the constitution without leaving any provision for the public schools, except such as the legislature will in its discretion provide. Others think that this is dangerous, and that provision will have to be made making it obligatory on the legislature to provide for the public schools and in that way avoid pressure on the legislature should hard times be the cry.

Saturday Deputy Sheriff John Black of Colleton county, accompanied by Special Deputies J. L. B. Warren, D. P. Patterson, Jr., S. W. Rivers, J. M. Patterson and F. L. Glover came to Columbia via the Coast Line bringing with them six negro prisoners from Waterboro, who a mob of men from Hampton county were preparing to lynch. The negroes are: Wm. Blake, Wm. Frazer, Cato Graves, Prince Graves and William Dix, Sr., who are charged with the murder of Mr. Meares, who was killed in his barn yard in Hampton county about a week ago. Three of these men have confessed the murder. They were confined in the Colleton county jail for safe keeping, and with them was W. C. Mimms, who is accused of killing Capt. Mixson, in Hampton county about a year ago. He was convicted at the February term of court, but was given a new trial on a technicality, and at the June term his case was continued because of the death of his lawyer.
cato-graves-waterford-1895-08-24.A3:
ROPES FOR SIX.
How a Lynching Party at Walterboro Was Foiled.
COLUMBIA, S. C., Aug. 24. — There are six happy negroes in Columbia today if no more, although all of them are in the penitentiary. In fact they are so glad they are living that they can hardly contain themselves. These men were brought here yesterday from Walterboro to escape an angry mob which was bent on stringing the whole outfit to so many trees, or so many limbs of the same tree, as the case might be. They and the officers who brought them here had a long exciting and dangerous run through swamps and woods and had to row several miles down a river before they were safe from the infuriated crowd.

Over a year ago in Colleton County a negro named W. C. Mimms, brutally murdered a white man named Mixson. He was convicted but got a new trial. The second trial was to have come up this summer, but owing to the death of his attorney the hearing was postponed until fall. Several weeks ago a white man named Meares in Hampton County was wantonly and maliciously butchered for the purpose of robbery. Five negroes were arrested on the charge, their names being William Blake, William Frazer, Cato Graves, Prince Graves, and William Dix, Jr. The murder caused intense excitement among the people and for reasons of safety all the prisoners were taken to the Walterboro jail.

On Thursday it became rumored about the town that a mob was coming in that night to lynch the sex-
the pursuing crowd evidently lost the trail after the fleeing party got the boat, and the deputies finally landed safely at the railroad bridge across the river several miles from where they started. The Charleston and Savannah fast mail was due soon after their arrival at the bridge, and taking the bridge keeper's lantern, the deputies waved the train down, boarded it and brought the prisoners to Charleston. From there they were brought to Columbia yesterday morning and by Gov. Evans' orders were put in the penitentiary for safe keeping. It was an exciting race for the deputies and hours of agonizing suspense for the prisoners, and no wonder that they are the happiest negroes in South Carolina today.—Columbia Register.

NEWS SUMMARY. MONDAY, AUGUST 19.
STATE—On Sunday, August 18th, it was very warm.—Cokesbury District W. M. S. closed its annual meeting.—John Bowick committed suicide at McCormick. Disagreement with his children said to be the cause.

On Monday, Clemson students publish denial of recent reflections on that college and its managers in The State. R. W. Simpson does the same in Anderson People's Advocate. Cadets will again have dress uniforms.—Women suffragists will be in Columbia during the Convention to try and secure their wishes.—Extra dispensary constables in Charleston.—After three days' test, the Port Royal dock is reported to United States government as a success.—W. W, Hodges's nomination for Probate Judge of Newberry confirmed by a close vote.

NATION—On Sunday, 18th inst., seven drowned at Ocean City, Md., by overcrowding and upsetting a little boat.—Several others drowned throughout the country, two of them on the way to church in W. Virginia.—Railroad wreck at Toccoa, Ga. Expressman, Walter Greer, of Kingville, S. C., killed.—Valkyrie III reached New York.—Sam Lewis, white, lynched in Florida. He was a native of Vermont, and had killed nine men.—Explosion in a Denver hotel destroyed many.

On Monday, Ex-Justice Wm. Strong, of the Supreme Court, died.—The Denver explosion killed 25 people.—Steamer Childs ordered released.—Wages of 5,000 miners in Michigan increased.—Small fire in the Johns Hopkins University.—Twenty-seven Spring Valley riots (Italians) sent up for trial for beating and driving away negroes.—Liberty Bell will go to Atlanta on October 4th.—Electrical storm at Pittsburg destroys property and life.

WORLD—On Sunday, 18th, it was intensely hot in Europe.—Emperor William II laid foundation of monument to his grand-father Emperor William I.—Japanese defeat Black Flags in Formosa and end the rebellion.—As set off to German celebrations, the French publish accounts of German cruelties in late war.—China doing little to further inquiry into massacre.—In Germany hard feeling against England is shown.—Socialist in prison defeats Prince Odescalchi for deputy in France.

On Monday, sharp earthquake in New Zealand.—Armenians are in great destitution. Kurds taunt them with valuelessness of European protection.—China refuses to allow inquiry by commissioners at Ku Cheng.—French gunboat will go 1,000 miles in China.—Nihilists blew up Torla Barracks, Russia, killing 300.—Lord Wolseley is made English commander-in-chief.—Parliament adopts closure rule.

TUESDAY, AUGUST 20.

STATE—Election of delegates to Constitutional Convention. Very light vote and little interest. Nominees of primary elected.—A. J. Blowers, of Spartanburg, died at Glenn Springs.—Tow-boat Maryland and scow No. 3 sunk in Charleston harbor.—Asylum insufficient for the insane.—Eastover reports first bale new cotton. Sold at 7 1/2 cts.

NATION — Atlanta Fair managers have wisely withdrawn bull fight they had arranged.—Georgia Supreme Court decides scalpers' tickets are good.—Florida lynchers acquitted.--Appointment of minister Rdnsom decided illegal.—Memphis has her first bale of cotton.

WORLD—Chinese officials refuse to allow foreign consuls to be present at Tu Cheng inquiry. Consuls protest.—Sultan again refuses European demands for Armenia.—J. W. Louther, husband of Salisbury's niece, made deputy speaker and chairman of committees.

WEDNESDAY, AUGUST 21.

STATE—Nominees of primary elected

elected over State, except in Beaufort, which elected Republicans.—Hot spell broken by rains.—Master J. F. Redding, Jr, saves H. Dierenbecker from drowning on Sullivan's Island.—Gen. S. D. Lee visits Abbeville to meet kinsmen.

NATION—Ex-Gov. Jas. E. Campbell nominated for governor of Ohio and the Convention holds to gold basis.—N. C. & St. L. Railway will form association to compete with Southern Freight Association.—Man killed at Social Circle, Ga., Saturday night last, thought to be from Charleston.—United States will endeavor to secure presence of our consul at Ku Cheng inquiry.

WORLD—Rioting among Germans at Mulherin, Germany, and Bene, France.—Dispatch to London, says officials at Chengtu are implicated in massacre; and inquiry as it is conducted will do nothing. Methodists ask protection.

THURSDAY, AUGUST 22.

STATE—Col. John T. Sloan, long clerk of House of Representatives, died. The government will test right of Clubs to keep liquor, and issues warrants for eleven members of Columbia Club and their servants; and Club men move before Judge Simonton.—Body of John Saba, drowned by sinking of Maryland, found.—Successful tobacco "break" held at Darlington.—Coast Line train runs from Rockey Mount, N. C., to Florence, 173 miles, in 3 hours and 27 minutes, stopping twelve times.—G. L. Davis, Rock Hill, commits suicide.

NATION—Less than a third who paid income-tax have filed claims for its return.—Seven men of American Railway Union finish sentence and are released.—Negro murderer lynched in Arkansas.—Ex U. S. Senator Conger, of Michigan, lives in Washington in destitute circumstances.—Train robbed in Nebraska.—Architect, superintendent, builder, foreman and inspector of New York collapsed building, arrested.—First international yacht race fixed for Sept. 7th.—Clyde steamer Comanche successfully launched.—Winston rioters punished by varying sentences.

WORLD—American mission at Fuchau destroyed and missionaries barely escape. Anti-foreign feeling very strong. Highest officials implicated in Ku Chung massacre. Chinese circulate pamphlets to inflame populace.—England will move vigorously to protect missionaries.—Commons discusses bi-metallism and Armenian outrages.—Earl Cadogan, Ireland's viceroy, enters Dublin.—Earthquake in Malaga, Spain.—Cholera deaths in Japan reach 16,830.—Mujigo, Culan, shot to death.

FRIDAY, AUGUST 23.

STATE—Sergeant Moorhcad, of the Columbia police, suspended—Body of infant found near Brailsford plantation, near Summerville. Infanticide suspected.—Rumored that a lynching party was formed in Hampton county and was foiled by removing the murderers of R. Mears.—The Port Royal dock must be strengthened.

NATION—Gov. Culberson says he will prevent the prize fight at all hazards.—Nominations for officers of new State of Utah are being made.—Cardinal Gibbons returned from Rome.—Minister Denby, at Peking, moves too slowly to please our government and Eustis seems imprudent.—Complete list shows 25 persons perished in Denver hotel fire.--Business good.

WORLD—China appointed Liu Ping Chang, recognized instigator of anti-foreign feeling, as imperial commissioner in Ku Cheng inquiry.—Small rebellion crushed and leader arrested in Spain.

SATURDAY, AUGUST 24.

STATE—Constable Eichelberger suspended under charges of unbecoming conduct.—H. A. Nagel, of Charleston, commits suicide in Washington.—South Carolina Commandery Knights Templar leaves for triennial conclave in Boston.—W, B. Welsh murdered at Haile gold mine by Charlie Loyd, colored.

NATION—M. W. Ransom, U. S. minister to Mexico, having been declared illegally appointed by Acting Assistant Attorney General, there is doubt of his reappointment.—Knights Templar begin to assemble in Boston.

WORLD—No news from Ku Cheng.—Baron Warlegg urges European police supervision in China.—Assault made by two Chinese on American missionary at Tung Chau.—Cholera spreads in Corea. Tarsus outrage was serious and will be investigated.—Japanese dismantling and evacuating Port Arthur.--Thousands of French soldiers sick in Madagascar. 25,000 pilgrims are at shrine of Lourdes. Effort to blow up Baron Rothschild injures his clerk.—English Liberals re-organizing.

frank-maxwell-augusta-1895-08-28.A1:
SHOOTING AT AUGUSTA.
An Escaped Negro Convict Killed by a Policeman.
An Escaped Negro Convict Killed by a Policeman.

Augusta, Ga., Aug. 27.—A fatal shooting affair occurred this morning about daylight during the attempt of two policemen to arrest an escaping convict.

Policemen Dave Murphy and John Reynolds were on duty on a dark side street and saw a man ahead of them hurrying along with a bundle on his shoulders. In all such cases their orders are to stop the parties, and unless they give a good account of themselves to send them into headquarters.

This man, when told to halt broke into a run. The policemen gave chase. Murphy played out, but Reynolds finally caught the fellow. The negro, for such he proved to be, fought him like a tiger. They fell to the ground and the policeman felt himself being overpowered. He drew his pistol and fired. The negro them jumped up and ran. About this time Murphy came up again and renewed the chase. The darkey dodged into a yard and ran under a house. They dislodged him and he broke off down the street again. As Murphy was still within ten or twelve feet of him the negro yelled, "If you come to me I'll kill you."

Saying this he stopped, and the policeman also stopped. Then the negro started toward the policeman, and Murphy said: "Halt, if you don't, I'll shoot you," but the negro didn't halt, and the policeman fired.

The man fell to the ground and in a few minutes died. When they examined him he was found to be a convict named Frank Maxwell, who had escaped from the county gang at the junction of Twiggs and Campbell streets. He had on the county stripes.

Maxwell was a notorious chicken thief and has been on the gang more or less for ten or fifteen years. The coroner's jury returned a verdict of justifiable homicide.

To-night a negro carpenter, Gibbes Heyward, went to take a dose of quinine, and took strychnine instead. He is now at the negro hospital in a precarious condition.

The Charleston Young Men's Christian Association base ball club came to Augusta to-day for the game that was prevented by rain ten days ago. They brought an excursion of Charlestonians with them, and Augusta turned out enthusiastically for the game. There were fully three three thousand people at the game, which resulted in a victory for Augusta by a score of 5 to 2. The Augusta rooters are making merry to-night, parading the asphalt with a bass drum, flying colors and victorious college yells.
frank-maxwell-augusta-1895-08-28.A3:
THE NEWS IN BRIEF.
THE NEWS IN BRIEF.

Condensed Account of Important Events From All Over the World.

A holiness convention will be held at Durham, N. C., beginning Sept. 17.

The Odd Fellows of North Carolina will erect a new orphanage at Goldsboro.

Two North Carolina negro convicts made a break for liberty and were shot and killed by the guards.

Seab Wilson, of Gadsden, Ala., committed suicide because his wife ran away with another man.

Selma (Ala.) has a new steamer which will ply the river trade. The Josie W. makes her first trip this week.

The Heflin (Ala.) Gold Mining company has been organized, with headquarters at Chattanooga, Tenn.

Dr. R. L. Vaught of Chattanooga, Tenn., was drowned, accidentally, at Point Pleasant, W. Va., Wednesday.

Dr. Robert Battey, the world renowned surgeon and specialist, of Rome, Ga., is in a low state of health.

The gas plant at St. Augustine, Fla., is being greatly enlarged to supply the increased demand in that growing city.

William H. Hanford, a Georgian employed in the government printing office at Washington, has become insane

Near Marianna, Fla., the little son of H. L. Smith killed his 13-year-old sister while playing with a pistol supposed to be unloaded.

Policeman Murphy of Augusta, Ga., shot and killed an escaped negro convict named Frank Maxwell, who was resisting arrest.

At Millen, Ga., the Millen and Stillmore Telephone company opened their 36-mile telephone line, which connects Millen with Stillmore.

The governor of South Carolina is about to take steps to correct the violation of the law by cotton mills working over 11 hours per day.

The Buckeye marble mills, at McMillan's Station, Tenn., nine miles from Knoxville, were burned. Loss, $10,000. Fully insured.

North Carolina negroes are holding meetings all over the state in the interest of an exhibit for the Cotton States and International exposition.

The question of the constitutionality of a city ordinance which prohibits women from entering saloons at Thomasville, Ga., is being agitated.

At Jacksonville, Fla., R. V. Connerat of Savannah, broke the southern bicycle record of 2.10 1-2. George N. Adams is the holder of the state championship.

W. H. Flowers of Boling, Ala., one of the state's oldest citizens, is dead. He was the largest lumber manufacturer in the state, and had amassed a large fortune.

Octavius Coke, secretary of state, died at his home in Raleigh Friday afternoon after over five weeks' illness of typhoid fever, during nearly all of which time he was delirius.

The Georgia crop bulletin for the week reports cotton much damaged by the recent heavy rains which have been general. Corn is, also, showing some signs of too much wet weather.

Jacksonville, (Fla.,) was the hottest place in the Union last Sunday, with a single exception; Bismarck, N. D., being 1 degree higher. It was 95 in the former and 96 in the latter.

Near Agate, Ga., Harvey Wilson, white, stabbed his stepfather, Thomas Montgomery, a number of times in the chest and on the arms, inflicting dangerous and possibly fatal wounds.

The Afro-American Press association of Alabama meets in its first annual session in the First African Methodist Episcopal Zion church in Birmingham, Thursday, and will hold for three days.

A negro excursionist on his way to Aiken, S. C., from Charleston, fell between the cars at Montmorenci, on the South Carolina and Georgia railroad and was killed. The negro was drinking.

Governor Evans may take charge of the police force of Columbia, S. C. Recent raids on the clubrooms of the city have caused trouble in the department over the enforcement of the dispensary law.

Georgia's new rate of taxation has been fixed at 4.56 mills. Last year it was 4.37 mills. The increase was necessitated by the shrinkage of values in taxable property since the last rate was fixed.

A ballot is being conducted through the columns of a Jacksonville, Fla., paper upon the Sunday closing of saloons. The latest issue places the vote at 682 for closing and 664 against Sunday closing.

David Click, proprietor of Click's hotel at Newport, Tenn., in attempting to get out of the way of a slowly moving freight train, fell under it, and received injuries from which he died in an hour.

At Luverne, Ala., a negro was caught in the quicksand at the bottom of a well and, for 48 hours was held fast in spite of all efforts to relieve him. When, at last, he was rescued, he was almost dead.

President Diaz of Mexico, has declined the invitation of the Cotton States and International exposition to visit the show, on the ground that the law forbids his leaving the country during his term of office.

The Florida pardoning board has granted a pardon to Henry Stephens of Madison county, who was convicted at the spring term, 1895, of the circuit court of horse stealing and sentenced to one year in the state penitentiary.

Congressman Bankhead of Alabama

jim-cullins-lynchburg-1895-08-24.A1:
ASSAULTED A POLICEMAN.
A Negro Perhaps Fatally Wounded While Resisting a Lynchburg Officer.
LYNCHBURG, VA., Aug. 24.—Police Officer J. R. Coomes, of this city, shot and probably fatally wounded to-night a colored man by the name of Jim Cullins. The negro resisted arrest, and striking the officer in the face with, it is thought, a pair of knucks attempted to throw him over the railing of a foot bridge, on which they were standing. Coomes fired four times, two balls taking effect.

A JAIL DELIVERY.
Six Negroes Make Their Escape From the Monticello Jail.
Monticello, Ark., Aug. 19, 1895.
—Saturday afternoon, while Deputy Sheriff Walter Wilson was feeding the prisoners at Monticello, he was attacked and overpowered by the prisons and six negroes escaped. Wilson whose pistol had been taken from him by the negroes, soon gave the alarm and the town people promptly set to work for their capture. They were overtaken several blocks from the jail and made to stand, threatening to shoot if their pursuers advanced. Messrs. Jack Carey, Dave Mills, J. P. Burks and Jas. Bennet, the foremost of the pursuing party, continued to advance and the negro who had Wilson's pistol fired. Quite a number of shots were exchanged but no one was hit except Mr. Bennet, who received a flesh wound in the face. The prisoners were all captured except two. The negro shot Bennet is very desperate, and is now under arrest for the murder of a white man at Tillar some time last year. There was considerable talk of lynching him, but the more conservative element prevailed and he was quietly returned to jail.
jim-jones-monticello-1895-08-22.A3:
A BOLD BREAK FOR LIBERTY.
Four Drew County Jail Birds Sail out into Fresh Air.
And Two of Them are Still Sailing.
Last Saturday evening, about a quarter past seven o'clock, when Deputy Sheriff, Walter Wilson, wont up in jail to feed his prisoners, he was no little surprised to find himself suddenly in the grasp of a burly negro, who was in jail for murder. Assisted by other inmates, Mr. Wilson was soon relieved of his pistol, and four prisoners, all negroes, made out of jail and toward the Western suburbs of the town. Mr. Wilson followed, immediately, raising the alarm, keeping close up with Jones, who had his pistol, and was in jail awaiting trial for the brutal murder of a white man near Tillar, last spring, by the name of Beltzhoover. Mr. Wilson was soon joined, in the chase, by Mr. James Bennett, of Dermott, and Mr. Zach Curry, of this city, when the negro came to a stop, and opened fire upon his pursuers. The negro fired four shots, one of which struck Mr. Jas. Bennett, in the jaw, inflicting an ugly flesh wound. Mr. Bennett fired five shots at Jones, none of which struck the mark. Jones was disarmed by Wilson and Curry and marched back to jail.

Bill Terrell, another of the prisoners, who was in jail for burglary and larceny, was captured, and safely escorted back to the bastile. The two others, made good their escape. Albert Collins, a mulato negro charged with outraging his step-daughter, was one to get away. The other was a boy, in jail for some trivial offense.

The prisoners had during the day, by some means, managed to remove the fastenings from their cell doors, and were thus enabled to rush into the corridor and overpower the jailor.

The wound which Mr. Bennett received, while quite painful, is only a flesh wound, and he is able to be up, and will soon be well.

During the fullisade between the negro and Mr. Bennett, Mr. D. S. Wells galloped up on horseback, with a shot-gun, and attempted to shoot the negro, but his horse thrown him, which no doubt saved Jones' life. Excitement ran high for a while.
jim-jones-monticello-1895-08-22.A6:
MURDERER JONES LYNCHED.
He Killed One Man, Shot Another and Broke Jail.

Little Rock, Ark., Aug. 22.—The negro Jones who murdered Whitman Belzove at Tillar some time ago, and who broke jail at Monticello a few days ago and shot James Bennett, a prominent young man, while resisting arrest, was lynched last night at Monticello by a mob of twenty-five men. The mob could not get the keys from Jailer Wilson and had to break into the jail. The negro was dragged out by the mob. He begged piteously for mercy, but he was only given a short time to pray. A rope was placed around his neck, and he was swung to a tree. His body was then riddled with bullets. It was left swinging and was cut down to-day.
jim-jones-monticello-1895-08-22.A17:
HANGED BY A MOB.
A Negro Taken From Jail at Monticello, Ark., and Lynched.

MONTICELLO, Ark., Aug. 23. —Wednesday night at 1:30 a. m. a body of about twenty-five men went to the jail here, broke the door down and took the negro, Jones, who broke jail last Monday, but who was recaptured before getting far. His body was found yesterday morning dangling from a tree not far from town. No clew to the perpetrators or participants in the lynching. Jones was locked up or charge of murder.
jim-jones-monticello-1895-08-22.A22:
Negro Lynched.
MONTICELLO, Aug. 23. — Yesterday morning at 1:30 o'clock about twenty-five men, masked and armed, broke open the Drew county jail with crowbars and other instruments and took W. A. Jones, a negro, from the jail and carried him to the suburbs of the town, where they hanged him to a limb. The mob held the jailer so that he was powerless to defend the jail or summon assistance. W. A. Jones maliciously and in cold blood murdered Harry Beltshoover in September, 1894, at Tillar, Ark., while latter was walking through his farm, in the presence of his wife. On Saturday, August 17, Jones, having secured the jailer's pistol, made his escape and shot James Bennett through the face while the latter was attempting to recapture him. The opinion rife in Monticello is that a mob from Tillar, Ark., lynched the negro because they regarded the jail insecure.
jim-jones-monticello-1895-08-22.A23:
THE lynching of the negro, Jones, at Monticello, Wednesday night, was uncalled for, and every man who participated in it has committed a crime against the laws of his State. Jones had killed two men and the certainty of his being convicted and hanged could not have been questioned. The desire to commit a lawless deed led the mob to take the prisoner's life, when he would have been executed by the proper authorities. Where is the excuse for such a crime as this mob committed? There is none. The mob ought to be apprehended and punished.—Ark. Democrat.

The Democrat is correct about it being wrong to mob the negro, Jones, but as the punishment, prescribed by law, for such an offense is hanging, of course the mob will never be punished.

Those engaged in the act should be heartily ashamed of it, for where mob-law prevails there is no law, and where there is no law there is no protection of life or property. It is always best to let the law take its course.
jim-jones-monticello-1895-08-22.A24:
break which Jones made on Saturday before, wherein he tried to escape and to murder innocent people led to the lynching. The people became alarmed lest he would escape and, probably, murder someone else, hence the mob-spirit was engendered which led to the unlawful tragedy of Wednesday night.

The lynchers, we understand, were mounted on horse back and the presumption is that they came from a distance; but as none of them were recognized this, of course, is only conjecture.

The body was taken down by the sheriff and given decent burial, after the Coroner's inquest had been held. Nothing was elicited before the inquest to implicate any one in the unlawful affair.

While Jones was a selfconfessed murderer, and there was no question of his guilt, it was wrong for the mob to take the law into their own hands, and there is no excuse for their conduct.

john-stromaa-wharton-1895-08-20.A1:
SAID HE ESCAPED.
Negro Murderer Is Probably Lynch ed by His Captors.
Wharton, Tex., August 19.—(Special.) —The escaped negro convict who murdered Deputy Sheriff Brown was captured by a posse last night, but they did not have him when they reached town today, reporting that he had "escaped." The chase for him has ceased.
john-stromaa-wharton-1895-08-20.A2:
MURDERER WAS CAUGHT
But is Said to Have Escaped From the Posse.
DETAILS OF THE ASSASSINATION
Confessed to Having Committed the Murder Not Yet Found.
Wharton, Texas, August E.—(Special Correspondence.)—The last details of the brutal murder of Deputy Sheriff Frank Brown by the negro convict yesterday is furnished by Sheriff Rich today. Justices Whitten held the inquest late in the evening. But little more of details is known at this hour (11 a. m.) From the sheriff is gathered the following: Last Thursday six convicts escaped from the Caney State farm, in Matagorda county. Information came to Sheriff Rich, who at once sent word to his deputies to keep a watch. Yesterday while Deputy Brown was at the home of his father-in-law, Andrew Kemp, twelve miles from this town, a negro came to the well for water. Deputy Brown being on the lookout for strange negroes, began questioning him. The negro told Brown that he was on his way to town; this among other things aroused the deputy's suspicion, and he told the negro that he would take him to town. The negro allowed himself to be handeuffed on one wrist, the deputy fastening his rope to his saddle, started to town, taking his shotgun. This was the last seen of Brown alive. The negro was not searched.

About 4 o'clock the driver of the Bay City mail hack found Brown lying dead in the road about five miles below town.

Sheriff Rich, from the inquest, draws out the following facts: It was evident that the negro had a pistol concealed. At a favorable opportunity, when behind the deputy, he drew his pistol and shot Brown in the back, the ball ranging in the region of the heart. Grabbing the deputy's shotgun, he fired again, the ball taking effect in the wrist. The ball cut out in the breast was a 32-caliber pistol. The bullets from the shotgun took effect in the back of the neck.

The more correct description of the man arrested is as follows: A dark brown-skinned negro, 5 feet 7 or 8 inches in height, weighs 165 pounds, appears to limp in one leg, wore laborer’s clothing. Another describes the man as above six feet in height, but bearing the same general description.

After killing the deputy the murderer turned his pockets, and taking his spurs, gun and gray mare, left at once.

Sheriff Rich has appealed to Governor Culberson to offer a reward for the murderer. Large posses of citizens of this county are searching the county.

The sad death of Frank Brown is felt deeply by every citizen of this county. He was a young man of worth, beloved and respected. He leaves a young wife and children and the sympathy of our people go out to them in this, their sad bereavement.

12 noon—Mr. J. G. Barbee, who heads one posse, has just sent word to town that Frank Brown’s horse, saddle and bridle, all complete, showed up at Brown’s house this morning. Mr. Barbee sends for dogs to track the convict, who it is supposed, is still in the thickets.

Later—4 p. m.—Mr. J. G. Barbee and others have returned and the search is over. From him it is learned that Bob Golbraith, Banks Barbee and Albert Paul, taking up the trail of the murderer, came upon him last night gambling with other negroes on the lower Brooks place. They arrested and guarded him all night. They turned the prisoner over to another posse early this morning and the posse started to town with him, but on arrival here they reported that the prisoner had escaped. Constable Hearit, who has been very active in the pursuit, says as soon as he heard that the man was captured he rode hard to catch up with the posse and when he did they also affirmed that the prisoner had escaped. With Mr. Barbee the constable then returned to town.

The Post reporter learns from a gentleman just from the scene of the capture that the prisoner confessed to the mode and manner of killing Deputy Brown and also where he had hid the deputy's gun.

Various rumors are afloat, every one forming their own opinion. Sheriff Rich has been untiring in the search for the escape.

The last sad rites were held over the remains of the murdered deputy this evening, and all that was mortal of Frank Brown now rests at peace in the city cemetery.

W.F.L.
john-stromaa-wharton-1895-08-20.A4:
Killed His Captor.
WHARTON, Tex., Aug. 19.—News has just reached here of the killing of Frank Brown, a well known citizen of this county. Brown had captured an escaped convict and was on his way to town with the man. While on the way the prisoner got the advantage of him and killed Brown, taking off with him Sheriff Rich and a posse have gone in pursuit. The man is a mulatto and was sent from Lamar county on a charge of grand larceny. Sheriff Rich has offered $100 for his capture.
john-stromaa-wharton-1895-08-20.A5:
Was Not an Escaped Convict.
Wharton, Texas, August 22—It appea
Wharton, Texas, August 22.—It appears now, after thorough investigation, that the negro who was lynched Tuesday night below town for the murder of Deputy Brown, was not an escaped convict. Sergeant C. F. Patton of the State farm in Matagorda county, seeing the information of the negro's arrest published in The Post yesterday, to verify the report as to whether he was an "escape," in company with Sheriff R. A. Rich he repaired to the place where the body was buried and had it exhumed for identification. The sergeant was fully satisfied that the man was not an escaped convict, and wishes The Post representative to so correct it. The negro gave his name as John Stroman, and it now transpires that he was wanted in Brazoria county for horse theft, having, it is alleged, stolen the famous race mare Crazy Jane from W. F. Sweeney of Chance's Prairie, Brazoria county.

There is very little comment over the lynching. The citizens unanimously clear Sheriff Rich of any dereliction in the discharge of his duty in not gaining possession of the murderer. In fact, the crime was of such a brutal nature that the "unwritten law" was invoked and that ended it.
